title: Product Decision Journal
project: AI Services POC — BambooHR Consultant App

outcomes.title: Make design work in Claude Code legible and transferable
outcomes.reasoning: Designer transitioned from Figma to Claude Code. Two things were lost: (1) the visual canvas showing all artboards/branches/iterations at a glance, and (2) the ability to hand off a project file where a new designer can see everything that's been designed and understand why. Without these, a Claude Code project is opaque to anyone who wasn't in the original sessions.

evidence.quote: If I take over a project that another designer has worked on, I just want to talk to Claude and get answers on any questions I have: why things were done a certain way, what the decisions were at critical junctures.
A coworker was using a spreadsheet to keep track of ideas, experiments done, results found. My reaction was: I want to be able to ask Claude about this instead of looking through a spreadsheet.

outcomes.title: Reduce work around the work
outcomes.reasoning: The AI Services POC is building tools for BambooHR HR consultants who manage multiple clients. The core product question: can we make the consultant's daily workflow — switching contexts, managing payroll, onboarding, benefits — feel effortless? The app should disappear and let the consultant focus on their clients, not the tool.

opportunities.title: Consultants need a fast, intuitive way to switch between client workspaces
opportunities.reasoning: HR consultants manage 5-50 clients and switch between them frequently throughout the day. The core UX question: how does a consultant select which client they're working with? Must feel fast, professional, and not lose context when switching. Prototyped 6 approaches (A-F), narrowed to 3 active candidates (B, C, E).

opportunities.title: HRCs lose sight of plan progress when it scrolls out of chat
opportunities.reasoning: The #1 visibility gap: ActionCard renders inline in chat and scrolls away as conversation continues. HRCs can't monitor what the agent is doing without scrolling away from the conversation. Need plan progress AND chat visible simultaneously. Requirements: tiered visibility (milestones in chat, thinking expandable), auto+toggle behavior, pause/stop/edit controls, non-undoable action gates, plan history as archive, cross-client persistence.

evidence.quote: I can only look at it while it's running which is like 5 seconds.

opportunities.title: HRCs spend time manually prepping for client meetings
opportunities.reasoning: Before every client meeting, HRCs manually gather context — open BambooHR, check Salesforce tasks, review recent emails, look at project plan status. This is repetitive, time-consuming, and easy to miss things. If Pandopticon knows a meeting is coming, it should automatically synthesize a prep brief from all available context so the HRC walks in ready.

opportunities.title: Need to understand how Pandopticon connects to external systems
opportunities.reasoning: Pandopticon's value comes from synthesizing data across multiple systems of record. Without a clear integration map, it's hard to communicate the vision, plan API work, or prioritize which integrations to build first. Need a visual artifact that shows every system, its role, and whether Pandopticon reads, writes, or both.

opportunities.title: HRCs context-switch to Salesforce for task/deadline visibility and simple updates
opportunities.reasoning: Discovery revealed Salesforce's role is narrower than assumed — it's a task template engine and billing trigger, not the day-to-day planning tool. The Customer Profile Doc (Google Docs) is the real source of truth. Three pain buckets: (1) CRUD pain — too many clicks, confusing views. (2) Intelligence pain — can't see what's urgent across clients. (3) Duplicate work pain — HRCs maintain real plans in spreadsheets/slides then update Salesforce separately; templates are outdated and require heavy editing. Salesforce does handle: deal-close billing triggers, client-to-HRC assignment (Katie), pre-loaded task templates per project type, hours spent/saved tracking. Katie wants but doesn't have: a dashboard tracking progress across projects and who's falling behind.

evidence.quote: Consultants maintain real plan in spreadsheets/slides, then update Salesforce separately. Feels like duplicate work.
Pre-loaded templates are old and outdated, requiring heavy manual editing every time.
Not a good way to present a project plan to customers — Thomas builds his in a slide deck.

opportunities.title: HRCs manually glue together 5 tools after every client call
opportunities.reasoning: Discovery workflow mapping revealed the core 'work around the work': after every client call, HRCs manually copy Attention insights into the Customer Profile Doc (Google Docs), update the project plan spreadsheet (Google Sheets), sync changes to Salesforce, and prep for the next call by re-reading all three. This manual glue work repeats for every client every week. The Customer Profile Doc (Google Docs) is the real source of truth — not Salesforce. Five tools in the daily loop: Attention, Google Docs, Google Sheets, Salesforce, ChatGPT. Pandopticon's job is to eliminate the manual steps between them, not replace any single tool.

evidence.quote: Single Google Doc which tracks: Customer info, Discovery call, Each call with transcription highlights from Attention. This is the real source of truth.
Build Project Plan Spreadsheet ~1hr

opportunities.title: No good way to share a project plan with clients that's easy to edit, easy to share, and looks good
opportunities.reasoning: HRCs need to share project plans with clients. The plan must be easy to edit, easy to share, and look professional. No current tool hits all three. Google Sheets: easy to edit and share, but not client-presentable. Google Slides: looks better, but hard to maintain — static snapshots that must be manually rebuilt after every change. Thomas builds plans in slide decks specifically because Sheets doesn't look good enough to show clients. Neither tool connects to the rest of the workflow — changes from meetings don't flow in automatically, and the HRC is the manual sync layer. The ideal: HRC edits conversationally via Pandopticon agent, Google Sheets is the backend (source of truth), and the client sees a beautiful always-current rendered view.

evidence.quote: Not a good way to present a project plan to customers — Thomas builds his in a slide deck.
Build Project Plan Spreadsheet ~1hr

opportunities.title: Project plan dates live in Google Sheets with no visibility or live link in Pandopticon
opportunities.reasoning: HRCs build project plans in Google Sheets and share them with clients. These are living documents — due dates shift constantly based on client conversations. A one-time import (S13) goes stale immediately. The AI agent can't prioritize work correctly with stale dates. HRCs won't re-import after every change. Pandopticon needs a live link to Google Sheets that stays current and can write back date changes captured from meetings (via Attention). The Google Sheets API supports full read/write, and OAuth is shared with Calendar/Gmail (BHR is a Google Workspace shop).

opportunities.title: Designers can't see the landscape of what's been explored
opportunities.reasoning: In Figma, you copy an artboard and start changing it — the canvas shows the whole train of thought, the branches, dead ends. In Claude Code, there's no equivalent. You can't see what screens exist, what was tried, what was abandoned. The mental model lives only in the designer's head and the conversation history.

opportunities.title: No institutional memory — new designer can't understand why things are the way they are
opportunities.reasoning: When a designer takes over a project, step one is knowing what exists (inventory). Step two is understanding why decisions were made (narrative). The previous designer might not be around to explain. Today there's no artifact that captures this — you'd have to read through every conversation transcript.

solutions.title: Plan Panel — Approach A: Right Rail (side panel)
solutions.reasoning: Resizable panel to the right of chat (420px default), modeled on ArtifactPanel. Has a collapsed floating pill with progress ring when minimized. Rejected because it's visually identical to Approach C (split view) — both are right-side panels. No meaningful UX difference from the user's perspective. Architectural difference (page-level vs ChatView-internal) doesn't matter to the HRC.

solutions.title: Plan Panel — Approach B: Sticky Dock (top bar)
solutions.reasoning: Collapsible bar pinned above chat messages. Collapsed: 60px with status dot, title, progress bar, controls. Expanded: ~200px with step list and agent log. Zero horizontal space cost. Genuinely different UX from the side panel approaches. Parked because: interesting pattern that could work on client home pages for cross-client plan visibility, but for the chat view the split panel (C) gives more room for detail. May come back for dashboard/home use.

evidence.quote: B is interesting, and we might be able to use that on the client home page actually when a plan is running.

solutions.title: Plan Panel — Approach C: Split View (internal to ChatView)
solutions.reasoning: ChatView splits into two resizable panes — chat left, plan right (380px default). Internal to ChatView so page layout sees no change. Natural transition: when no plan is active, it's a single pane. Chosen because it provides the most detail space alongside chat, feels like a natural extension of the conversation, and the resize handle gives the HRC control.

solutions.title: Design Iteration Tracker (Tool 1)
solutions.reasoning: A visual tool for tracking the branching tree of ideas during active design work. Shows what's active, parked, rejected, and how ideas spawned from each other. This is the 'Figma canvas replacement' — externalizing the mental model of exploration. Addresses OP1 directly.

evidence.quote: It's just hard to keep the whole tree in your head of good ideas vs ideas to come back to later vs rejected ideas.

solutions.title: Product Decision Journal (Tool 2)
solutions.reasoning: A living record of the entire product discovery process — outcomes, opportunities, solutions, experiments, decisions. Claude maintains it automatically. Primary interface is conversational (ask Claude 'why did we choose X?'). Secondary interface is visual (OST graph). This is the handoff artifact — makes a project legible to newcomers. Addresses OP2 directly.

evidence.quote: The mental model I have here is automated AI meeting notes, where AI has listened to the meeting and captured todos, action items, etc.

solutions.title: Approach A: Card Grid — full-page client cards with click-to-enter
solutions.reasoning: Full-page grid of client cards. Click a card to enter that client's workspace. Good first impression and onboarding feel, but mode-switch friction persists — you leave the workspace to see the grid. Parked because the cards metaphor has potential on the main dashboard page or combined with another approach, but not as the primary client selector.

evidence.quote: The clients as cards view is interesting, but I don't know if this is the right place for it. I could see it coming back on the main dashboard page, or maybe we like this + another idea.

solutions.title: Approach B: Dropdown Switcher — compact dropdown in tab bar
solutions.reasoning: Compact dropdown trigger in the tab bar area. Open to search/switch clients. Attention indicator on trigger shows pending items. Minimal space usage, fast switching, ⌘K hint for power users. One of two front-runner approaches.

solutions.title: Approach C: Sidebar List — persistent collapsible client panel
solutions.reasoning: Persistent sidebar (w-56, collapsible to w-12) with client avatars, names, unread badges, urgency indicators, and search. Fastest switching — client is always one click away. Collapsible to reclaim space. The other front-runner approach.

solutions.title: Approach D: Breadcrumb Navigation — hierarchical nav with admin table
solutions.reasoning: Breadcrumb trail (All Clients > Client Name) with a filterable/sortable admin table for client selection. Good triage tool but killed because there's only one layer of breadcrumbs, so the pattern doesn't justify itself.

evidence.quote: Kill. It's only one layer of breadcrumbs.

solutions.title: Approach E: Tab Groups — multi-client grouped tabs in a single bar
solutions.reasoning: All clients' chat tabs visible in one bar, grouped by client with colored headers. Each group has a client avatar chip followed by that client's chat tabs. Interesting Chrome-like model. Not a front-runner but kept open out of curiosity to see if it can be made to work at scale.

evidence.quote: This one has promise, maybe just because of a perverse curiosity I have to see if it could be made to work. It's not a front runner but we could come back to it.

solutions.title: Approach F: Client Tabs Row — horizontal avatar row above tab bar
solutions.reasoning: Row of client avatar circles above the chat tab bar. Click avatar to switch client context. Killed because it's essentially a two-layer tab (avatar row + chat tab bar) and the designer doubts HRCs will embrace circles as client identity.

evidence.quote: Kill. It's basically like a two-layer tab. I don't think HRCs are going to be keen on the circles to represent clients.

solutions.title: Project Plan Import & Timeline on Client Home Tab
solutions.reasoning: Full-width Project Plans section on client home tab with: (1) AI-powered import from pasted text/files via /api/extract-plan, (2) expandable inline timeline with phase blocks, milestones, today marker, (3) date confidence indicators (exact/inferred/ambiguous) with inline resolution UI, (4) AI memory injection — plan context appended to chat system prompts so the AI references upcoming milestones and deadlines. Mock data uses real Ashtead PM plan on Black Mesa + fictional plan on Aperture Science. Empty state CTA for clients without plans.

solutions.title: Calendar Integration + Meeting Prep Agent + Proactive Briefing Flow
solutions.reasoning: Three-part feature: (1) Calendar integration surfaces upcoming meetings on dashboard and client home — next meeting badge, countdown, attendees. (2) Meeting Prep Agent (agent-meeting-prep) generates context briefs by synthesizing client data, recent activity, open tasks, and project plan status. (3) Proactive briefing flow — 'Prep for meeting' button on client home triggers auto-creation of a chat with the meeting prep agent, pre-loaded with client context. The agent responds with a structured brief covering recent changes, open items, talking points, and post-meeting actions.

solutions.title: Attention.tech as meeting intelligence source (replaces/augments Google Meet/Zoom)
solutions.reasoning: Attention (attention.tech, now attention.com) is an AI meeting recording and intelligence platform. It records calls on Zoom/Meet/Teams, transcribes, and produces structured extractedIntelligence — action items, next steps, decisions, competitor mentions — pre-labeled and CRM-mapped. This is significantly richer than relying on Google Meet/Zoom's basic structured summaries. Key context: BambooHR already runs Attention — no licensing or procurement needed, just API access. Two integration paths: (1) Direct REST API — Pandopticon's backend calls api.attention.tech/v2/ (API key auth, well-documented endpoints for conversations, calendar, transcripts, extracted intelligence). Same integration pattern as Salesforce/Calendar. (2) MCP server — an official open-source Attention MCP server exists (17 read-only tools), but requires Claude as the model powering Pandopticon's agents (currently GPT). Recommended approach: REST API for structured data pulls (dashboards, client home, scheduled syncs), agent-accessible tools for conversational queries ('what did we discuss about dental plans last Tuesday?'). No Attention→Salesforce auto-sync — Pandopticon reads from both sources directly, so auto-sync would create duplicates rather than add value. Testing: connect to BHR's production Attention instance (read-only access, no sandbox concept, low risk).

solutions.title: Google Docs integration — read/write Customer Profile Doc (the real source of truth)
solutions.reasoning: Discovery revealed the Customer Profile Doc (Google Docs) is the real source of truth per client — not Salesforce. A single doc per client accumulates customer info, discovery notes, and Attention call highlights from every meeting. The Google Docs API supports full read/write (OAuth 2.0, shared with Sheets/Calendar/Gmail). Two high-value paths: (1) Write — auto-append Attention call summaries after every meeting, eliminating the most repetitive step in the weekly HRC workflow (~20 manual copy-paste sessions/week for a 20-client HRC). (2) Read — ingest the Profile Doc to dramatically enrich prep briefs and agent context with the HRC's own accumulated notes. Append-to-end is the safest write strategy (character-index-based API, but appending avoids position fragility). Transition path: Pandopticon starts by serving the doc → Client Home gradually becomes the better version of it → eventually HRCs stop opening the doc.

evidence.quote: Single Google Doc which tracks: Customer info, Discovery call, Each call with transcription highlights from Attention. This is the real source of truth.

solutions.title: Live Google Sheets linking for project plans (dynamic sync + write-back)
solutions.reasoning: Replace one-time plan import (S13) with a live link to Google Sheets. HRCs link a client's project plan spreadsheet; Pandopticon reads it via Google Sheets API, uses LLM to extract tasks/dates/milestones from varied spreadsheet formats, and keeps data current via hybrid freshness (post-meeting re-read + daily sync). Write-back enables the closed loop: Attention captures 'push open enrollment to April 15th' from a meeting → Pandopticon matches it to the plan → agent proposes update → HRC approves → API writes new date to the shared sheet → client sees it immediately. Auth is OAuth 2.0 shared with Calendar/Gmail. Key consideration: the sheet is client-facing, so write-back must be precise (correct cell, no formatting corruption) and the approval step is non-negotiable.

solutions.title: Approach A: Pandopticon-hosted rendered site for client-facing project plans
solutions.reasoning: A read-only web page generated from the Google Sheet plan data. Client gets a bookmarked URL. Pandopticon reads the sheet, renders a polished timeline/milestone view with BambooHR branding, keeps it current. Full design control, always live, mobile-friendly. The HRC never opens the spreadsheet — they edit via agent conversation in Pandopticon chat, the agent writes to Sheets (source of truth), and the rendered site updates automatically. One sentence from the HRC → three surfaces update (Sheet, Pandopticon views, client site). Security via unguessable token URLs or simple auth. Seeds the path toward a full client portal (Approach D). This is the recommended approach — it solves all three requirements (easy to edit via chat, easy to share via URL, looks good via rendered design) without changing the HRC's workflow.

solutions.title: Approach B: Auto-generated Google Slides from Sheets data
solutions.reasoning: Pandopticon reads the Sheets plan, generates a polished Slides deck via the Google Slides API. HRC edits in Sheets, client sees Slides. Stays in Google Workspace, clients already know Slides. But: Slides API is fiddly for layout, static snapshots that need re-generation after every change, not truly live, not great on mobile. Decent interim if the hosted site feels like too much infrastructure too soon.

solutions.title: Approach C: Branded PDF auto-generated after each plan update
solutions.reasoning: Every plan change triggers a polished PDF dropped in a shared Drive folder or emailed to the client. PDFs look professional and are universally accessible. But static — stale immediately, clients accumulate versions, no on-demand status checking. Better as a complement to a live view than a standalone solution.

solutions.title: Approach D: Client portal within Pandopticon
solutions.reasoning: A stripped-down authenticated view where clients log in and see their project plan, milestones, recent updates, meeting summaries, document links. The fullest vision — exactly what Katie said she wants ('clients could log in and see progress against project plan'). Too much scope for now (needs client auth, permissions, user management), but this is the long-term direction. Approach A (rendered site) naturally grows into this over time. Deferred, not rejected.

evidence.quote: Future feature (not built): Clients could log in and see progress against Project Plan

solutions.title: Approach E: Notion page (auto-synced from Sheets)
solutions.reasoning: Pandopticon pushes plan data to a Notion page per client. Beautiful out of the box, shareable via URL, clients can comment. But adds Notion as a dependency, another tool in the stack, doesn't brand as BambooHR. BHR may not want to adopt Notion org-wide.

solutions.title: Approach F: Email digest after each milestone or plan change
solutions.reasoning: Send the client a beautiful HTML email when the plan changes: 'Here's where your project stands.' Visual timeline, what's done, what's next. Meets clients in their inbox, no URL to remember, creates a communication touchpoint. But not interactive — client can't check on-demand. Works best as a complement to a live view (Approach A), not a replacement. Notify via email, link back to the live URL.

solutions.title: Integration Map — visual diagram of all system connections
solutions.reasoning: HTML diagram showing Pandopticon's relationship to 10 systems of record: BambooHR (Core, R+W), Google Calendar (Exploring, R), Google Meet/Zoom (Exploring, R), Attention.tech (Exploring, R), Google Docs (Exploring, R+W), Google Sheets (Exploring, R+W), Salesforce (Exploring, R+W), Google Drive (Exploring, R), Gmail (Exploring, R+W), Slack (Exploring, R+W). Sandwich layout with SVG-drawn read/write connection lines. Uses real brand logos. Living document — updates as integration status changes.

solutions.title: Salesforce as intelligence layer data source + agent write-back
solutions.reasoning: Follows the established intelligence-layer pattern (same as calendar, Meet, Gmail). Three capabilities: (1) Read — pull tasks, deadlines, case status into dashboard, client home, and prep briefs as another data source. No new Salesforce tab. (2) Surface — enrich existing views with Salesforce context (e.g., 'Client has 3 overdue tasks' on client home, task deadlines in prep briefs). (3) Write-back via agents — 'mark this task complete,' 'log this meeting note' so HRCs don't context-switch for simple updates. Feasibility assessment: straightforward if staying in the intelligence layer. The integration pattern (read→synthesize→surface) already exists for BambooHR and calendar. POC implementation is ~1-2 days: mock salesforce-data.ts, add Tasks section to client home, feed into prep briefs, add agent write-back. Production considerations: Salesforce OAuth is non-trivial, and org-specific custom objects/fields require a flexible mapping layer.

solutions.title: Key decision: Two separate tools, not one
solutions.reasoning: Tool 1 (iteration tracker) is the workbench — used during active design. Tool 2 (decision journal) is the archive — used for handoff and institutional memory. Tool 1 feeds into Tool 2: exploration captured in the iteration tracker gets distilled into the decision journal as entries. They must stay separate because they serve different audiences and timescales. The iteration tracker can be referenced from a decision journal node but they have independent schemas and lifecycles.

experiments.title: Spreadsheet for tracking decisions
experiments.reasoning: A coworker's approach — tracking ideas, experiments, results in a spreadsheet. Rejected because: not queryable conversationally by Claude, not visual/spatial, flat structure can't represent an OST hierarchy, and the designer's reaction was 'I want to ask Claude about this, not look through a spreadsheet.'

experiments.title: Obsidian vault (folder of markdown files)
experiments.reasoning: One file per decision/opportunity/experiment, linked with [[wikilinks]]. Good for humans browsing, good for Claude to read/write. Rejected because: Obsidian's graph view is famously useless for comprehension (hairball), requires Obsidian as a dependency, and adds friction to adoption.

experiments.title: Single structured JSON + standalone HTML viewer
experiments.reasoning: Chosen for v1. Claude reads/writes JSON natively. Zero external dependencies — render it however you want with a standalone HTML file (proven pattern from the iteration tracker). JSON isn't fun to read raw, so it lives or dies by the viewer and Claude's ability to answer questions from it. Simplest path to a working v1.

experiments.title: Single markdown file with conventions (DECISIONS.md)
experiments.reasoning: Headings = outcomes, subheadings = opportunities, bullets = solutions. Claude can read/write trivially, humans can read in any editor. Rejected because: too unstructured for reliable querying, no graph view possible without a parser, and markdown conventions drift over time.

experiments.title: Notion as collaboration layer
experiments.reasoning: Notion databases can represent the OST relationally (Outcomes, Opportunities, Solutions, Experiments as linked databases). Multiple views of same data (kanban, table, gallery, timeline). Real-time collaboration built in. Official Notion MCP exists with full read/write (22 tools, create entries, update properties, write page content). Free plan works for solo + 10 guests. Deferred because: collaboration isn't a v1 requirement, and the local JSON approach proves the concept faster. But this is the path forward for scaling across the org.

evidence.quote: Official Notion MCP server, maintained by Notion. Setup is one command + OAuth. Claude can create databases, create entries, update properties, write page content. Cannot upload files or do bulk operations.
Unlimited pages and blocks for solo use. Databases and API fully available. Up to 10 guest collaborators. Pain points: 5MB file cap, 7-day version history, 1000 block limit for team workspaces.

experiments.title: Hybrid: local JSON + Notion sync
experiments.reasoning: Claude maintains a local JSON copy for querying and reasoning. Periodically syncs to/from Notion for collaboration. Trio maintains their FigJam OST, Claude reads it via MCP, reconciles with local copy. Described as 'janky but interesting' — doesn't require the trio to change behavior. Deferred to post-v1.

experiments.title: SQLite database
experiments.reasoning: Structured and queryable, Claude can read/write via bash. Powerful for complex queries. Rejected because: invisible without a viewer, overkill for most projects, adds complexity without proportional benefit over JSON for this use case.

experiments.title: Git-native approach (commit history + PR descriptions)
experiments.reasoning: No new artifact — decisions live in commit messages, PR descriptions, branch names. Claude synthesizes on demand. Rejected because: most commit messages are garbage, only works retroactively, and doesn't capture the reasoning/context that lives in conversation.

decisions.title: Prune client navigation prototypes: keep B, C, E — park A, kill D and F
decisions.reasoning: After building and reviewing all 6 client-selection approaches at v3 with full-width tab bars, the designer pruned the set. B (Dropdown) and C (Sidebar) are the strongest candidates — both switch-first approaches that feel fast for daily workflow. E (Tab Groups) stays open as an intriguing experiment. A (Card Grid) is parked — the cards-as-clients metaphor has potential but may belong on the dashboard, not here. D (Breadcrumb) is killed — only one layer of breadcrumbs, so the pattern doesn't add value. F (Client Tabs Row) is killed — essentially a two-layer tab with avatar circles; HRCs unlikely to embrace circles for client identity.

evidence.quote: A: park. The clients as cards view is interesting, but I don't know if this is the right place for it. I could see it coming back on the main dashboard page.
D: kill. It's only one layer of breadcrumbs.
E: this one has promise, maybe just because of a perverse curiosity I have to see if it could be made to work.
F: kill. It's basically like a two-layer tab. I don't think HRCs are going to be keen on the circles to represent clients.

decisions.title: Plan panel: kill A, park B for home page, ship C (split view)
decisions.reasoning: Built 3 plan panel approaches (A: right rail, B: sticky dock, C: split view). A and C were visually identical — both right-side panels, just different render locations. Killed A. B (dock) is genuinely different UX (horizontal bar, zero horizontal cost) but limited detail space. Parked B with the insight that it could work on client home pages for cross-client plan visibility. Chose C (split view) for chat because it gives the most detail space and feels like a natural extension of the conversation.

evidence.quote: Get rid of A. B is interesting, and we might be able to use that on the client home page actually when a plan is running. So park it for now and we'll continue with C.

decisions.title: Claude auto-maintains the journal via implicit capture
decisions.reasoning: The 'AI meeting notes' model: Claude watches for decision moments in conversation and logs them automatically. The designer doesn't change their behavior. Explicit capture ('/decision' command) also available as a supplement. Hook-based capture (post-session review) is interesting for later. The key insight: the tool fails if it requires manual curation — it needs to be passive like meeting notes AI.
openItems: Exact trigger heuristics for implicit capture not yet defined
Post-session hook design not yet specified

decisions.title: Notion is the collaboration path, but not v1
decisions.reasoning: The scaling story: (1) Now: local JSON, solo + conversation with Claude. (2) Soon: show the workflow works, org buys Notion, sync local journal to Notion. (3) Later: standardized template, every project gets an OST workspace. Collaboration is not a v1 requirement, but the architecture should point toward it. The designer is pioneering a process to scale across the org.

evidence.quote: Collaboration is not a hard requirement for v1, but I'm pioneering a process here that I would really like to be able to scale across the org.

decisions.title: Establish 12px floor and 12/13/14/16/20/24 type scale
decisions.reasoning: Font audit found ~60% of visible text was 10-12px. Nav labels at 10px, step numbers at 11px, status badges at 10px — all below comfortable reading size. Established 12px as the minimum floor. Buttons bumped from 12px to 13px with font-semibold to give them more visual weight for decision-critical actions (Approve/Decline on payroll plans). Custom text-[10px] and text-[11px] classes replaced with text-xs (12px) throughout. Compact step indicators kept at 10px as the one exception (tiny circles need tiny text).

decisions.title: Project plans live on client home tab with inline expandable timeline
decisions.reasoning: Plans surface as compact cards in a full-width section between Recent Chats/Active Plans and Recent Activity. Click to expand inline timeline (not a separate page/panel). This keeps plans contextual to the client without adding navigation layers. The timeline uses phase-colored left borders, milestone bullets, a today marker, and amber highlights for ambiguous dates. AI extraction handles the import (GPT parses phases/milestones/dates from pasted text), with a mock fallback for demo reliability.

decisions.title: Meeting prep is proactive and agent-driven, not a static page
decisions.reasoning: Instead of building a 'meeting prep page' that the HRC navigates to, the prep brief is generated on-demand by a specialized agent in a chat. The HRC clicks 'Prep for meeting' on client home → a new chat opens with the Meeting Prep Agent → the agent synthesizes all available context into a conversational brief. This means the HRC can ask follow-up questions, drill into specifics, or request changes — it's interactive prep, not a static document.

decisions.title: Pandopticon is an intelligence layer across all integrations — never the system of record
decisions.reasoning: Same principle applied universally: BambooHR owns HR data, Salesforce owns tasks/cases, Google Calendar owns schedule, Gmail owns email, Slack owns messages, Drive owns files. Pandopticon reads from all, synthesizes context, surfaces insights, and can write back simple updates (mark task complete, draft reply) — but never becomes where the data lives. This avoids the maintenance trap of rebuilding each system's CRUD and keeps Pandopticon focused on the intelligence gap between systems. Refined in D10: this extends to files — Pandopticon links to files in their source systems rather than hosting copies. The UX for managing linked files is an instance of a broader agent context management problem (Q12).

decisions.title: Pandopticon is an orchestration/intelligence layer, not a file host — pull context, don't store files
decisions.reasoning: Files already have homes (Google Sheets for plans, Google Docs for profile docs, Google Drive for policies). The value isn't the file — it's the intelligence about the file ('open enrollment is due in 4 days'). Uploading files to Pandopticon creates stale copies — the exact anti-pattern that led us to live Google Sheets integration over one-time import. Discovery confirmed: HRCs have their files organized in Google Workspace. The pain isn't 'I can't find my files' — it's 'nothing connects my files to my meetings to my tasks to my deadlines.' Pandopticon reads from source systems via API and surfaces intelligence. Fallback: if API access is blocked (OAuth approval, IT gatekeeping), manual import is a degraded mode (S13 already built). The UX for linking files will feel similar to hosting files — HRCs need to manage what files are connected to each client, which files agents have context on. But the underlying architecture is links and reads, not uploads and storage. The bigger frame: HRCs need a way to manage agent context — what data the scheduling, prioritization, and project management agents can see. File linking is one instance of this; other instances include which Salesforce tasks, which Attention recordings, which Google Docs to include. This is a general UX problem: agent context management.

decisions.title: The ideal end-state is FigJam OST with Claude read/write
decisions.reasoning: If Claude could write to FigJam, the solution would be obvious: trio maintains OST in FigJam (as they should already be doing), Claude reads and writes via MCP, humans see it natively, no duplicate work. Currently blocked by FigJam MCP being read-only. This is the north star — every intermediate solution is a stepping stone to this.

openQuestions.title: Can the plan dock (Approach B) work on the client home page?
openQuestions.context: Designer noted the sticky dock pattern could show running plans on client home/overview screens, not just inside chat. Would give cross-client plan visibility without navigating into a chat. Worth exploring when we build the client home page.

openQuestions.title: What are the exact heuristics for implicit decision capture?
openQuestions.context: Claude needs to recognize decision moments in conversation: 'let's go with X', 'that doesn't work because...', 'oh interesting, what if...'. What patterns trigger a journal entry vs. are just normal conversation?

openQuestions.title: What should the OST graph viewer look like?
openQuestions.context: User wants a node-and-edge graph (not just a card list). Should show dead ends grayed out, active paths highlighted. Needs to be zoomable/pannable. Should also collapse to a flat rich-content list. Standalone HTML, zero dependencies.

openQuestions.title: When and how to introduce Notion sync?
openQuestions.context: After v1 proves the concept. Needs: Notion MCP write working reliably, a database schema that maps to this JSON schema, a sync strategy (one-way push? bidirectional merge? conflict resolution?).

openQuestions.title: How does the trio's existing OST practice (if any) integrate?
openQuestions.context: Trios should be building OSTs. If they already are (in FigJam, Miro, etc.), the journal shouldn't duplicate that work. Ideal: Claude reads the trio's OST and enriches it with design-session details.

openQuestions.title: Should project plan import support PDF parsing natively?
openQuestions.context: Moot. The direction is live Google Sheets linking (S18), not file import. PDF parsing was relevant when we assumed plans would be uploaded to Pandopticon. With the 'pull context, don't host files' decision (D10), project plans stay in Sheets and Pandopticon reads them via API. Manual import (S13) remains as a fallback if API access is blocked, but investing in PDF parsing for a fallback path isn't worth it.

openQuestions.title: What does the post-meeting flow look like?
openQuestions.context: Designed. After a meeting: (1) Attention captures extractedIntelligence (action items, decisions, next steps). (2) Pandopticon reads it, matches items to existing client state. (3) Agent proposes updates: write date changes back to Google Sheets (project plan), append call summary to Google Docs (Customer Profile Doc), update action plans, create tasks, resolve open questions. (4) HRC approves → one write cascades to Sheet, Pandopticon views, and client-facing site. No auto-sync to Salesforce (Pandopticon reads both sources directly). Still needs to be built, but the design question is answered.

openQuestions.title: Should Salesforce integration focus on read-only or read+write?
openQuestions.context: Read+write, scoped. Discovery revealed Salesforce is a billing trigger and task template engine, not the daily planning tool. Read: pull task templates, deadlines, hours data. Write: sync status back so HRCs stop manually updating Salesforce after updating their spreadsheet. Not full CRUD — Pandopticon handles simple updates (mark complete, log note, push deadline) via agent write-back. The bigger question has shifted to Q13/Q14: how much project management should Pandopticon own, and how do we minimize double data entry if Salesforce stays in the picture.

openQuestions.title: What's the right integration priority order after BambooHR?
openQuestions.context: Ten systems now mapped (Google Docs elevated from Drive sub-item to its own integration). BambooHR is core. Discovery revealed the Customer Profile Doc (Google Docs) is the real source of truth — this makes Google Docs arguably the highest-priority integration after BambooHR. The Google Workspace cluster (Docs + Sheets + Calendar) shares one OAuth and covers the three most critical HRC workflows: client context (Docs), project plans (Sheets), and meeting scheduling (Calendar). Attention.tech feeds into both Docs (call summaries) and Sheets (date changes) — it's the input layer. Salesforce's role is narrower than assumed (task templates + billing, not daily planning). The most compelling integration story: Attention→Docs (auto-append call summaries) + Attention→Sheets (write back date changes) + everything→Client Home (unified prep view). Gmail and Slack remain passive monitoring. Google Drive is context enrichment for policies/SOWs.

openQuestions.title: Should Pandopticon's agents use Claude instead of (or alongside) GPT?
openQuestions.context: Currently agents use GPT (OpenAI). Switching to Claude (Anthropic) would unlock MCP — a protocol for giving AI models tool access to external systems. An official Attention MCP server exists (17 tools), and MCP servers exist for many other integrations (Notion, Salesforce, Slack, etc.). This is bigger than Attention — it's an architectural decision that affects how ALL integrations work with the AI agents. With Claude + MCP, agents could natively query Attention, Salesforce, Slack, etc. during conversation. With GPT, the same functionality requires wiring each integration as OpenAI function calls manually. Trade-offs: Claude MCP is more elegant and composable, but adds Anthropic as a dependency alongside OpenAI. Could also run both models for different agent types.

openQuestions.title: Should the app introduce a second typeface?
openQuestions.context: Font audit revealed the entire app uses a single typeface (ui-sans-serif system font stack). A second typeface — e.g., a geometric sans for headings or a monospace for data/metrics — would help differentiate content types (navigation vs. body text vs. numerical data). Not needed yet but worth considering as the UI matures. Could also help distinguish agent-generated content from user-authored content.

openQuestions.title: How do HRCs manage agent context? (What data do agents see per client?)
openQuestions.context: Pandopticon pulls context from source systems rather than hosting files (D10). But HRCs need to manage what's linked: which Google Sheets are the project plans, which Google Doc is the profile doc, which Salesforce tasks are relevant, which Attention recordings to include. This is file linking on the surface, but the deeper problem is agent context management — the HRC is curating what the scheduling, prioritization, and project management agents can see and reason about. The UX will feel similar to 'uploading files to a project' (familiar pattern), but the underlying operation is linking, not storing. Open questions: Should linking be per-client or per-agent? Auto-discovered or manual? What does the management UI look like on Client Home? How much should agents auto-discover context vs. wait for the HRC to explicitly link it?

openQuestions.title: How much orchestration/project management do HRCs need in Pandopticon?
openQuestions.context: Pandopticon is an intelligence and orchestration layer (D8, D10). But there's a spectrum: at one end, it just surfaces insights from other systems ('you have 3 overdue tasks'). At the other end, it becomes the place where HRCs actually manage projects — create tasks, assign owners, track progress, sequence work. Discovery shows HRCs currently do this across Sheets + Salesforce + Google Docs, poorly. The question: what's the optimal amount of project management to pull into Pandopticon? Too little and it's just a dashboard — useful but not indispensable. Too much and we're building a project management tool, which is a different product and competes with Salesforce. The sweet spot is probably: Pandopticon handles prioritization and judgement ('what should I do next across all my clients?'), orchestrates updates across systems via agents, and surfaces a unified view — but doesn't try to be the task CRUD layer. Related to Q14: if Salesforce stays as the task backend, how much PM does Pandopticon need to own?

openQuestions.title: If Salesforce stays as the task backend, how do we minimize double data entry and psychic damage?
openQuestions.context: Salesforce is entrenched — BHR uses it for billing triggers, task templates, hours tracking, and Katie's management oversight. Even if Pandopticon becomes the daily workspace, Salesforce probably doesn't go away. The risk: HRCs end up maintaining state in both places. Discovery already found this is the #1 pain — 'consultants maintain real plan in spreadsheets, then update Salesforce separately.' Pandopticon could make this worse (now it's THREE places) or solve it (Pandopticon as the single pane of glass that syncs to Salesforce automatically). Key strategies to explore: (1) Agent-mediated sync — HRC works in Pandopticon, agent writes status back to Salesforce automatically. (2) Salesforce as read-only input — pull templates and deadlines in, but stop asking HRCs to update Salesforce manually. (3) Replace Salesforce's task tracking entirely — if Pandopticon + Sheets handles project plans and the client-facing site handles client visibility, what does Salesforce still do that can't be moved? (4) Accept coexistence but minimize friction — auto-sync what can be synced, make the rest one-click from Pandopticon. The answer depends heavily on what Katie and BHR leadership are willing to change about their Salesforce usage.

openQuestions.title: How does the client-facing rendered site handle auth and security?
openQuestions.context: Approach A (S20) proposes a Pandopticon-hosted site where clients see their project plan via a bookmarked URL. Security options: (1) Unguessable token URLs (like Google Docs 'anyone with the link' sharing) — simplest, no login required, but anyone with the URL can view. (2) Simple auth — email + magic link, or password per client. (3) SSO tied to BHR's client portal if one exists. The right answer depends on how sensitive the data is (project plan milestones and dates, probably low sensitivity) and how much friction is acceptable for clients. Token URLs are probably fine for v1.

openQuestions.title: What's the relationship between the client-facing site and Katie's desired client portal?
openQuestions.context: Discovery surfaced that Katie wants 'clients could log in and see progress against project plan' (a future Salesforce feature that doesn't exist yet). The rendered site (S20) does exactly this — but outside Salesforce. Is S20 the seed of Katie's client portal? If so, it could grow to include meeting summaries, document links, progress history (Approach D / S23). This would give BambooHR a branded client-facing product that Salesforce can't deliver. Worth validating with Katie: would a branded project plan URL per client solve the client visibility problem she described?

evidence.quote: Future feature (not built): Clients could log in and see progress against Project Plan
